utterances.text: Welcome to Hard Times Unpacked — a close, unhurried look at one of Dickens's most urgent and unsettling novels.
Hard Times was published in 1854, and it has never stopped feeling like it was written about right now.
It is Dickens at his most compressed, most polemical, and — some would argue — most perfectly constructed.
Over this episode, we'll be pulling the novel apart — its language, its politics, its characters, its fury — and putting it back together again.
I'm joined today by three people whose company I'd choose for exactly this kind of conversation.
Dr. Eleanor Hartley is a novelist and creative writing teacher who thinks about how great fiction is built — the craft beneath the surface, the choices that look effortless but aren't.
Professor James Blackstone is a legal and social historian — he'll keep us honest about what Coketown actually was, what the law meant for the people living under it, and what the stakes really were.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has loved and argued with this novel since she was a teenager — she'll be our reader's conscience throughout.
Welcome, all three of you.
Let's start at the very beginning — because the opening of Hard Times is one of the great ambushes in English fiction.
Eleanor, you've taught this opening many times — what happens in those first pages?
What Dickens does in the first chapter of Hard Times is essentially commit an act of literary violence — and it's glorious.
We open in a schoolroom, and the first word that hits us is 'Facts.'
Gradgrind, the novel's great utilitarian schoolmaster, is delivering his philosophy before we even know his name.
The chapter is titled 'The One Thing Needful' — which is already a bitter joke, because that phrase echoes the Gospel of Luke.
In the Gospel, the one thing needful is spiritual attention — sitting at the feet of Christ. In Gradgrind's schoolroom, it's facts.
Dickens has set up his whole satirical project in a chapter title before a single character has spoken.
And then the prose itself enacts the philosophy — it's relentless, percussive, almost bullying in its repetition of that word.
'Now, what I want is, Facts. Teach these boys and girls nothing but Facts.'
That opening sentence is like a fist on a desk. You feel the authority in it — and the narrowness.
What always arrests me is the physical description of Gradgrind that follows — because Dickens doesn't waste a syllable.
The man is described as having a square wall of a forehead, and everything about him is square and hard and measuring.
His very name — Gradgrind — grinds as you say it. There's a kind of cruelty built into the sound.
And then there's the moment when a girl is called upon to define a horse, and she can't do it — she who clearly knows horses, loves them.
Her name is Sissy Jupe, but Gradgrind immediately renames her — calls her 'Girl number twenty.'
That detail breaks my heart every time. She has a name. She has a father. She has a whole inner life — and he reduces her to a digit.
And then a boy named Bitzer is asked the same question about a horse — and he reels off a textbook definition, bloodless and correct.
Dickens uses this contrast to say everything he needs to say about what systematic education destroys.
It's worth pausing on what Dickens was actually targeting, because there's sometimes a misreading of this novel as simply anti-intellectual.
He wasn't against education. He was against a very specific educational ideology that was gaining real institutional power in the 1840s and 50s.

The utilitarian reformers — followers of Jeremy Bentham and James Mill — genuinely believed that human beings were rational calculating machines, and that education should train that faculty and no other.
There were government inspectors visiting schools, insisting on rote learning and tested facts — it was policy, not caricature.
And Dickens had seen it. He'd reported on it. He'd watched what it did to children.

So when Gradgrind's schoolroom inspector — this figure called simply 'the gentleman' — praises Bitzer's horse definition and condemns any child who'd put a wallpaper pattern of horses in a room because 'you wouldn't paper a room with horses in nature' — that's almost verbatim from real inspectors' reports.
Dickens exaggerates for effect, as he always does. But the target is precise.
James's point about precision matters enormously when you look at the structure of the whole novel.
Dickens divides Hard Times into three books — 'Sowing,' 'Reaping,' and 'Garnering.'
Those titles are agricultural — biblical in register — and they work against everything Gradgrind stands for.
You can't measure a harvest the way you measure a fact. Growth is organic, unpredictable, seasonal — and so is moral consequence.
The book's architecture is itself an argument against utilitarian thinking — and that's the kind of structural wit that I find genuinely thrilling.
By the end of 'Garnering,' every seed Gradgrind planted has produced something he didn't want and can't control.
And those consequences land on his children — which is where the emotional centre of the novel sits, for me.
Louisa and Tom Gradgrind are raised on facts, starved of imagination, and the novel watches what that starvation produces.
Louisa in particular — she has this one extraordinary scene where she looks into a fire.
Her father asks her if she is considering his proposal that she marry Mr. Bounderby, a man decades her senior.
And she keeps staring into the fire — not answering — and she says the fire has been rising and falling since she can remember, and she wonders what it is, and where it goes.
It's a small moment, but it contains everything — her longing, her suppressed imagination, her inability to name what she feels because she was never taught she had feelings worth naming.
Gradgrind's system has worked — and that is the tragedy.
The marriage to Bounderby is worth dwelling on from a historical angle, because it illustrates something about property and personhood that the novel handles with great shrewdness.
Bounderby is not just an unpleasant husband — he is the self-made manufacturer, the industrial capitalist in his most pompous, self-congratulatory form.
His great myth — and Dickens hammers this — is that he was born in a ditch and raised himself by sheer will.
He repeats the story of his abandoned, impoverished childhood to anyone who will listen — and we eventually discover it is entirely fabricated.
His mother, Mrs. Pegler, turns up at the end of the novel — a respectable woman who raised him with care and sacrifice.
The lie of the self-made man. Dickens saw through it with absolute clarity — and he saw what that lie does to every person the man then employs or marries.

What's remarkable is how every thread we've pulled — the schoolroom, the marriage, the self-made myth — leads back to the same question: what happens when a system mistakes measurement for understanding?
And that question is at the heart of what we'll turn to next — how Dickens constructs his attack on utilitarian doctrine, and what weapons he chooses to do it with.

segments.title: The Utilitarian Machine: How Dickens Unmasks Social Doctrine

utterances.text: We've been talking about the opening assault of facts — the way Gradgrind's classroom operates as a kind of philosophical weapon.
Now let's go deeper into the doctrine itself — Utilitarianism as Dickens understood it, and what he thought it was doing to English society.
It's worth being precise about what Dickens is actually attacking, because he tends to get caricatured as simply anti-intellectual — an enemy of reason itself.

What he's targeting is a very specific application of Utilitarian philosophy — the version that had been industrialised, you might say, by political economists and factory owners in the 1840s and 50s.
The idea that you could reduce every human question — education, poverty, labour conditions — to a calculation of aggregate utility.
Dickens saw, with remarkable clarity, that this abstraction was not neutral — it systematically excluded the people who most needed to be counted.
The hands in Coketown are not persons in Gradgrind's ledger — they are units of production.
And Dickens embeds that dehumanisation in the very language of the novel — which is one of his great structural achievements here.
Think about the way Coketown is described — the town itself becomes an expression of the philosophy that built it.
Dickens writes that the buildings all looked alike — the jail, the infirmary, the school, the church — all built on the same model, all declaring: fact, fact, fact.
"It contained several large streets all very like one another, and many small streets still more like one another, inhabited by people equally like one another."
The repetition in that sentence — 'like one another,' 'like one another,' 'like one another' — it's the prose performing the grinding uniformity it describes.
Dickens is not just reporting on the Utilitarian world — he is making you feel what it is like to live inside it.
What strikes me every time I re-read this novel is how funny it is — and how that humour is itself a kind of argument.
Dickens doesn't just show us the Utilitarian system — he makes it look absurd.
Think of the government inspector, Mr. M'Choakumchild — even the name is a small act of violence.
And then there's the scene with Sissy Jupe — girl number twenty — who cannot define a horse to Gradgrind's satisfaction.
Bitzer gives the definition: "Quadruped. Graminivorous. Forty teeth, namely twenty-four grinders, four eye-teeth, and twelve incisive."
It's technically correct and utterly hollow — and Dickens makes you feel that hollowness like a physical absence.
Sissy has grown up around horses — she loves them — and she cannot speak.
The system has made her knowledge invisible because it cannot be formulated.
That contrast between Sissy and Bitzer is one of the most precise things in the novel — it runs all the way through to the end.
Bitzer is the system's perfect product — lean, self-interested, drained of all colour — and Dickens literally describes him that way.
He writes that the light of the classroom fell on Bitzer and showed him to be so light-coloured that he looked almost transparent.
Against Sissy, who is dark-eyed and warm — suffused with the vitality that her circus world has given her.
It's a moral taxonomy rendered in physical description — Dickens using the body as an index of character in the most deliberate possible way.
And the irony — the devastating irony — is that when Gradgrind's own children need saving, it is Sissy who saves them, not Bitzer.
The system eats its adherents and is rescued by the one it was designed to consume.
What I want to press on is how Dickens constructs Gradgrind himself — because he's a more interesting figure than he sometimes gets credit for.
The name is so perfectly ugly that it risks becoming a cartoon — and yet Dickens gives him genuine conviction.
Gradgrind believes.
That's what makes him tragic rather than simply villainous — he is not cruel, he is catastrophically wrong.
Dickens signals this right at the opening — Gradgrind's very physicality is a diagram of his philosophy.
"A man of realities. A man of facts and calculations. A man who proceeds upon the principle that two and two are four, and nothing over."
The staccato rhythm of those short declarative sentences — 'a man of realities, a man of facts' — it enacts the very reduction it describes.
Dickens is doing something extremely sophisticated: the style of the description mimics the style of the man being described.
And then there's Bounderby — who is a very different kind of critique, and in some ways even more damning.
Gradgrind at least is sincere — he genuinely wants to improve human welfare through his principles, however wrong-headed those principles are.
Bounderby uses the same philosophical language — self-help, industry, independence — but he is an absolute fraud.
His whole identity is a manufactured myth — the self-made man who was found in a ditch, raised himself by his bootstraps.
And the revelation that his mother has been there all along — respectable, loving, quietly surviving — is one of the great comic deflations in Victorian fiction.
He is forever declaring that the workers want to be fed with turtle soup and venison out of gold spoons.
"What I know is, that these people are utterly unreasonable and entirely incompatible with the progress of society."
That phrase — 'incompatible with the progress of society' — Dickens is skewering the way ideology licenses contempt.
It still sounds terrifyingly familiar.
The Bounderby unmasking is historically very pointed — Dickens knew exactly what he was doing.
The Self-Help mythology — Samuel Smiles published his famous book in 1859, just a few years after Hard Times — was the ideological glue that held the whole system together.
If anyone could rise through industry and virtue, then poverty was simply a moral failure — and those at the bottom deserved to stay there.
Dickens shows us the lie inside the logic.
Bounderby didn't rise from nothing — he had a mother, a home, a start — and he has spent decades erasing that history to serve his own vanity and his class interests.
The myth of the self-made man was always partly self-serving mystification — and Dickens anatomises it with surgical precision.
There's one more structural element I think we have to name — and that's the novel's chapter titles.
Dickens titled his three books 'Sowing,' 'Reaping,' and 'Garnering' — a deliberate agricultural metaphor in a novel set in an industrial city.
That choice alone tells you something about his argument — that the Utilitarian factory has replaced an organic relationship between human beings and their world.
What you sow, you reap — but in Gradgrind's system, what you sow is abstraction and what you reap is devastation.
Louisa and Tom are the harvest — and they are catastrophically poor harvests.
Which brings us, rather naturally, to Louisa herself.
Because if Gradgrind's system has a most eloquent victim, it might be his own daughter — a character who has so thoroughly learned not to feel that she barely knows how to speak.
That silence — what it costs, and what it finally breaks — is where we're headed next.

segments.title: Louisa's Silence: The Language of Emotional Starvation

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Dickens dismantles the utilitarian machine at the level of doctrine and institution.
But the most devastating damage that machine does is interior — and nowhere is that more visible than in Louisa Gradgrind.
Louisa is, for me, the true centre of the novel — the character in whom Dickens's argument becomes unbearably personal.
She's been so thoroughly trained out of feeling that she can barely name what she's missing.
There's that extraordinary early scene where she and Tom are watching the fire through the Gradgrind parlour window.
She says something like — wondering, as she's gazed at the fire so often, what the fire would look like and suggest to a heart that could not be reasoned into ashes.
That word 'ashes' does so much work — it's what her own heart has been reduced to, and she knows it, and she can't say it plainly.
The fire is the only image of passion and warmth available to her, and she can only approach it through a hypothetical — through wondering what it would be like if she were allowed to feel.
What Caroline's putting her finger on is a brilliant piece of narrative engineering — Louisa's emotional life is expressed almost entirely through indirection.
She cannot speak her feelings directly because she has no language for them — her father's education has seen to that.
So Dickens finds this extraordinary solution: he gives her the fire, the stars, the distant smoke — physical things that carry the feeling she can't articulate.
Think about the moment before she agrees to marry Bounderby — one of the most chilling proposals in English fiction.
She asks her father: what does it matter, and then: I have not much feeling remaining, but I am not quite without it.
That's the most devastating acceptance speech you'll ever read — a woman consenting to her own extinction.
And Gradgrind, fatally, takes it as consent — because the utilitarian calculus has no category for what she's actually telling him.
Historically, Gradgrind's response is entirely within the legal and social norm — a daughter's consent was frequently a formality, not a negotiation.
What Dickens is exposing is that the utilitarian framework and the existing marriage law are perfectly aligned — both treat women as units in a transaction.
But the really precise historical observation Dickens makes is about education — or rather its systematic absence.
Gradgrind's children are educated in facts and nothing else — and there were real schools in the 1850s run on exactly these principles.
James Kay-Shuttleworth and the whole utilitarian school inspectorate believed that cultivating imagination was a waste of a child's cognitive resources.
Louisa isn't an exaggeration — she's a case study.
And yet she is also, paradoxically, one of the most feeling characters Dickens ever created — which is the awful irony.
She hasn't been made feelingless — she's been made mute.
The crisis — when she comes home to her father after the near-affair with Harthouse — is the passage I find almost unbearable.
She says: I have grown up, and the ground on which I stand has been robbed from under me.
And then — and this is where it breaks — she collapses at his feet.
She has spent the entire novel trying to speak and finally she cannot — her body says what her language never could.
That collapse is the most articulate moment she has in the whole book.
That scene is such a carefully structured catharsis — Dickens has been withholding that emotional release since the first chapter.
Notice how he uses Gradgrind in that moment — the father who built the prison is now forced to witness the prisoner break.
Gradgrind says something remarkable: he has a misgiving that some change may have been slowly working itself in his daughter since he had heard of her being in that other town.
A 'misgiving' — that's all his system allows him: not grief, not guilt, but a vague epistemological unease.
Dickens is being ferociously precise — Gradgrind's vocabulary is his character, and it cannot accommodate what is happening to his daughter.
There's a broader social point embedded there too, which is that the novel's men — Gradgrind, Bounderby — simply do not have the conceptual equipment to understand women's interior experience.
This wasn't accidental — the culture systematically denied that women had inner lives that required accounting for.

Sissy Jupe is interesting in this context because she comes from a completely different tradition of knowledge — circus, imagination, feeling — and she is the one who ultimately saves Louisa, not any of the men.
Dickens is quite radical there — he's suggesting that the alternative to the utilitarian system is not another intellectual system, but something more like love and instinct.
Sissy is Louisa's conscience and her compass — and their relationship is the emotional warmth the novel otherwise almost entirely withholds.
But I want to stay with what Louisa doesn't get — the ending Dickens gives her is devastating in its restraint.
She never remarries, she never recovers the life that was taken from her — she simply endures, more wisely.
Dickens writes that she is not unkindly called an old maid, and that children love her — which is about the most heartbreaking consolation prize in English fiction.
He can imagine her survival — he cannot quite imagine her flourishing.
That's the honest melancholy at the novel's core — Dickens shows the wound but he doesn't fully trust the cure.
Louisa's final fate is really a structural admission: some damage cannot be fully undone.
The system left its mark in the most intimate place possible — in how she relates to time, to hope, to other people.
Louisa starved of feeling, Gradgrind starved of imagination — and beneath all of this, another stratum of suffering entirely.
Coming up, we turn to Stephen Blackpool — a man who inhabits the same Coketown walls but finds the system has an entirely different kind of cruelty reserved for him.

segments.title: Stephen's Broken Promise: Class, Injustice, and the Coketown Walls

utterances.text: We've been talking about Louisa's silence — the way feeling is starved out of her almost before it can form.
But Hard Times gives us another kind of suffering entirely — less internal, more brutally exposed to the world.
Stephen Blackpool, the hand in Bounderby's mill, is the novel's portrait of working-class life at its most undeserved and most dignified.
His story turns on a promise he makes — or rather, is forced to make — and what that promise costs him.
Let's dig into Stephen's world — what Dickens is doing with this character, and why it remains so unsettling.
Stephen Blackpool is extraordinary because Dickens places him at the precise intersection of every trap the Victorian system had set for men like him.
He's locked in a miserable marriage he cannot legally dissolve — divorce being available only to those with money enough to pursue a Parliamentary Act.
He's in love with Rachael, a woman of extraordinary moral steadiness, and he cannot be with her.
When he goes to Bounderby — his employer, his social superior — to ask about the possibility of divorce, the scene is almost comic in its cruelty.
Bounderby essentially tells him: the law exists for gentlemen.
For a man like Stephen, the institution of marriage is a permanent cage — and the law is the lock.
And Dickens renders that cage with a very specific architectural image — the Coketown setting itself.
The town is described as a place of machinery and tall chimneys, where the piston of the steam-engine worked monotonously up and down like the head of an elephant in a state of melancholy madness.
"the piston of the steam-engine worked monotonously up and down, like the head of an elephant in a state of melancholy madness."
That image is doing something remarkable — it turns industrial machinery into a creature in torment.
The machine isn't just mechanical — it's suffering, endlessly, without purpose or relief.
That is Stephen's life, rendered in stone and steam before we even meet him properly.
What strikes me every time I re-read Stephen is how quietly Dickens insists on his dignity.
He never rages. He never becomes a symbol of class rebellion.
Stephen's great phrase — the one he returns to again and again — is simply: 'it's aw a muddle.'
"It's aw a muddle."
Three words, in his Lancashire dialect, and they carry the whole weight of a life the system has made incoherent.
He can't understand why his world is the way it is — and crucially, neither can he be given any satisfying answer.
Dickens refuses to give Stephen — or us — a tidy ideological solution.
That refusal is politically interesting, and historically contentious.
The Trades Union organiser, Slackbridge, is portrayed as a windbag and a bully — which infuriated many of Dickens's contemporaries on the left.
Stephen refuses to join the union — and this is where the promise becomes so devastating.
He has promised Rachael — for her sake, out of love — that he will hold himself apart from the union and from all agitation.
And the result is that he is ostracised by his fellow workers — called a 'knobstick' — and then let go by Bounderby as well.
He belongs nowhere. The promise that was meant to protect his relationship destroys his livelihood.
The irony Dickens constructs there is almost too painful to examine directly.
Stephen's loyalty — his one redeeming act of personal devotion to Rachael — is the very mechanism of his destruction.
And what I love, from a craft perspective, is that Dickens doesn't editorialize.
He does in the Coketown chapters precisely what he does with Gradgrind — he lets the structure of the situation make the argument.
The system punishes Stephen for joining the workers. The system also punishes Stephen for not joining the workers.
That's not muddle — that's a trap with no door.
And there's the scene with Rachael at Stephen's bedside — his drunken wife having nearly poisoned herself — which is one of the most quietly luminous scenes in the novel.
Rachael keeps watch through the night, and Stephen looks at her and thinks of her almost as a guiding star.
Dickens writes of her as Stephen's angel — 'thou art an Angel' — and the register shifts almost to prayer.
"Thou art an Angel."
It's so simple it could be embarrassing — but it isn't, because we've seen what this woman has done for him through the night.
The sentiment is earned by the scene. That's the difference between sentimentality and genuine feeling.
What strikes me about Rachael is that she represents an alternative ethic entirely — one based on care, on constancy, on showing up.
The novel is full of systems — Gradgrind's Fact, Bounderby's self-made-man mythology, the union's rhetoric.
And Rachael simply — quietly — refuses all of them.
She's not naive about Stephen's situation. She sees it clearly.
But her response to 'aw a muddle' is not ideology — it is presence.
And then Stephen's death — down the Old Hell Shaft — is handled with such controlled anguish.
He's dying, having been falsely suspected of the bank robbery, and he sees a star from the bottom of the pit.
He describes it as having been with him all through the night — echoing Rachael, calling her to mind even in his last moments.
Dickens writes something like: 'It ha' shined upon me in my pain and trouble down below.'
"It ha' shined upon me in my pain and trouble down below."
The dialect makes it achingly tender — this is a man who has nothing except his faith in Rachael's goodness, and he dies holding it.
I cannot read that scene without feeling the full weight of how the novel has prepared us for it.
The 'Old Hell Shaft' — even the name is doing moral work.
It's an abandoned mine — the detritus of industrial extraction, left uncovered, killing the man the industry has already discarded.
Dickens is not subtle there, and he doesn't need to be.
Stephen's last exoneration — Rachael and Sissy finding him, hearing his testament — feels both too late and exactly right for the kind of novel this is.
Stephen Blackpool — trapped, ostracised, falsely accused, and dying in a pit that industry dug and forgot.
And yet his last words are of a star. Dickens gives him that.
You mentioned Sissy just now — and she is, in many ways, this novel's most subversive character.
Coming up, we turn to the circus world she comes from — and to the magnificent comic catastrophe of the Pegasus's Arms and Sleary's philosophy.

segments.title: Comic Relief and Catastrophe: Sissy and the Escaping Horse

utterances.text: We've been sitting with the weight of Stephen's story — the walls that close in on the working poor.
But Dickens, being Dickens, never lets that weight become suffocation — he keeps a door open to the circus.
And at the centre of that opening stands Sissy Jupe — and the question of what happened to her father.
Sissy is one of those characters who arrives quietly and then, the more you think about her, the more extraordinary she becomes.
She enters the novel as a child of the circus — her father is Signor Jupe, a performer who dresses a performing dog and rides a horse called Merrylegs.
And then her father simply — vanishes.
He goes out one night, ostensibly to fetch some medicine for the dog, and never comes back.
There's something almost unbearably delicate about how Dickens handles that disappearance.
We never know whether he abandoned her or whether shame at his own failing powers simply drove him away.
What strikes me structurally is that the disappearance is never resolved — it's one of the novel's genuine open wounds.
Dickens gives us Sissy's interpretation, which is heartbreaking in its loyalty: she believes her father will return.
She keeps a bottle of nine oils — a remedy she associates with him — as a kind of secular relic.
But the novel never confirms or denies her hope, and that silence is structurally doing enormous work.
It positions Sissy as the novel's great keeper of unverifiable faith — which is precisely what Gradgrind's system cannot tolerate.
The social reality behind that vanishing is worth pausing on.
Circus performers in the 1850s occupied a genuinely precarious position — itinerant, outside any legal protection, entirely dependent on physical capacity.
When Signor Jupe's abilities begin to fail him, he has no trade union, no poor relief easily accessible, no recourse of any kind.
Dickens understood this acutely, which is why the circus folk are presented as their own community — a mutual-aid society operating entirely outside the factory system.
Sleary's troupe looks after Sissy without a second thought.
There's a pointed contrast there with every institution the novel shows us in Coketown.
And Sleary himself is one of literature's great small triumphs, isn't he?
The man has asthma and a lisp, he smells permanently of brandy, and yet Dickens makes him the novel's moral spokesman.
His great speech — his philosophy of entertainment — comes near the end of the novel, and I find it genuinely moving every time.
He says something to the effect that people must be amused, that they can't be always a-learning nor yet they can't be always a-working.
Through the lisp and the brandy fumes, Dickens is delivering his central argument about what human beings actually need.
What's technically brilliant about Sleary is that the lisp forces you to read him slowly.
The distorted spelling — 'thith' and 'thquire' — creates a kind of friction on the page.
And Dickens uses that friction deliberately — you cannot skim Sleary's speeches.
His truths arrive with difficulty, which is part of the point: wisdom doesn't come from fluent, polished Gradgrind-style declarations.
It comes up through the body, through imperfection, through life as it is actually lived.
I want to come back to Merrylegs for a moment, because that horse matters more than it might seem.
The animal apparently escapes with Signor Jupe — or at least disappears at the same time.
There's a tragicomic quality to that: a man and his performing dog and a horse, all vanishing into the night.
But it also connects to the novel's opening joke — the famous exchange about horses in the Gradgrind classroom.
Gradgrind demands a definition of a horse, and Bitzer obliges with something perfectly anatomical and entirely dead.
'Quadruped. Graminivorous. Forty teeth, namely twenty-four grinders, four eye-teeth, and twelve incisive.'
That's the Gradgrind vision of the world: complete, precise, and utterly incapable of including Merrylegs.
And Sissy is in the room when Bitzer recites that definition.
She's been asked first and she cannot answer — not because she doesn't know horses, but because she knows them too well.
She's grown up among them, loved them, watched her father work with them.
The Gradgrind definition excludes everything that makes a horse real to her.
That scene is comic on the surface — the pompous questioner, the stumped circus girl, the smug answer from the model pupil.
But underneath it is genuinely heartbreaking: a system that punishes embodied knowledge.
Sissy's trajectory through the novel is itself a kind of argument against Gradgrind's system.
She is a complete failure by his metrics — she never learns the statistics, the facts, the definitions.
And yet she is the only person in the novel who consistently acts with both warmth and effectiveness.
She comforts Louisa in some of the novel's most tender moments.
She faces down Harthouse — the smooth, cynical seducer — with a directness that stops him cold.
Dickens gives the moral victories to the girl who can't define a horse.
The Harthouse scene is worth dwelling on, because it's also quite funny in a dark way.
James Harthouse is one of Dickens's most cutting portraits of a certain kind of Victorian gentleman — bored, worldly, effortlessly charming, and entirely hollow.
He has talked his way through every social situation he has ever encountered.
And then Sissy walks in and simply tells him to go away — to leave Coketown and never return.
And he does.
There's something almost farcical about it — all that practised seduction undone by a circus girl's complete indifference to his social performance.
What moves me is that Sissy never becomes embittered by what the system does to her.
She absorbs the Gradgrind education, she fails it, and she comes out the other side still herself.
The circus — her origin, her father, Merrylegs, all of it — remains inside her, untouched.
I find myself thinking about the novel's closing image of her: surrounded by her own children, bringing imagination and warmth into the next generation.
She is, quietly, Dickens's answer to everything Gradgrind proposes.
Sissy as both comic creation and moral compass — it's a remarkable thing to hold together in a single character.
And it raises a question we haven't quite touched yet: how does the novel's form — its very architecture — participate in the argument it's making?
That's where we're heading next — the machinery of the narrative itself, and what Dickens built when he sat down to write this book.

segments.title: The Machinery of Narrative: How Form Mirrors Content

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Dickens uses his comic and tragic registers together — the circus folk as a kind of moral counterweight to Gradgrind's world.
That actually opens onto something I want to explore now: how the novel's very structure — the way it's built — enacts the argument it's making.
Eleanor, you've written about the architecture of Victorian fiction — where do you want to start with Hard Times?
The first thing you notice, if you're looking at the novel as a made object, is how unusually short it is for Dickens.
It was serialised in Household Words in weekly instalments, which is a completely different pressure from the monthly parts of, say, Bleak House or Dombey — you get much less room to breathe.
And Dickens turns that constraint into a formal principle — the novel feels compressed, almost machine-like in its economy.
The three books — Sowing, Reaping, Garnering — that's an agricultural metaphor, which is already doing something interesting in a novel about industrial capitalism.
You're meant to feel the irony: these are the rhythms of organic life imposed on a world that has abolished organic life.
The form is quietly arguing with the content from the very first page.
That division into three books does something else as well, historically speaking.
Sowing, Reaping, Garnering maps almost precisely onto the stages of a life under the utilitarian education system Dickens is attacking.
You sow the facts in children's heads — that's Gradgrind's school in Book One.
You reap the harvest of damaged adults — Tom's theft, Louisa's emotional collapse, the whole catastrophe of Book Two.
And in Garnering, you count the cost — what has been lost that can never be recovered.
The structure is itself a moral argument, laid out with rather terrible precision.
What strikes me as a reader is how that compression Eleanor mentioned affects the prose at the sentence level too.
Dickens in this novel writes with an almost percussive rhythm — short declarative sentences that hit like pistons.
Think of the opening of Chapter One — 'Now, what I want is, Facts.'
'Now, what I want is, Facts. Teach these boys and girls nothing but Facts. Facts alone are wanted in life.'
Three sentences, three hammers, and you know everything about Gradgrind before you've even been told his name properly.
The form IS the content — the relentless repetition of that word 'Facts' is itself a demonstration of the mind it describes.
Caroline has put her finger on something technically brilliant there — Dickens is using anaphora, the repetition of a word at the start of successive clauses, and it's completely deliberate.
Gradgrind's rhetoric has the structure of a machine — it repeats, it insists, it will not accommodate variation.
And then Dickens describes Gradgrind's physical appearance in terms that absolutely mirror that — the square finger, the square wall of a forehead, the square coat.
He is introducing a character by geometric reduction — the man has literally been squared off, all the rounded, human irregularity removed.
The narrator tells us his head was 'a man of realities, a man of facts and calculations' — and every physical detail is in service of that taxonomy.
It is satire as architecture — every brick placed to support the central thesis.
James, you study the real institutions behind these fictional ones — does the formal machinery of the novel correspond to anything in the institutional machinery Dickens is targeting?
It does, and in a rather precise way that I don't think gets discussed enough.
The utilitarian philosophy Dickens is anatomising — Benthamism, essentially — was itself a system that claimed to be able to reduce every human situation to a calculable quantity.
The 'greatest happiness of the greatest number' — which sounds benign — becomes in practice a justification for flattening individual suffering into statistics.
And the novel's structure — its relentless drive toward consequence, the way every seed sown in Book One must be reaped in Book Two — mimics exactly how utilitarian logic was supposed to work.

Except Dickens's point is that when you apply that iron causality to human beings, you produce not happiness but Louisa Gradgrind — emotionally starved, married off as a calculation, on the verge of ruin.
The system produces, with horrible efficiency, exactly what it claimed to prevent.
Louisa is the heart of the novel for me, structurally as much as emotionally.
There's that extraordinary scene where she's looking into the fire as a child, and her father catches her — just staring, lost in something she can't name.
And he rebukes her — 'What are you thinking, Louisa?' — as if imagination itself is a transgression in his house.
That image of the fire recurs throughout the novel — she watches it, returns to it — and it's the one place where her suppressed inner life flickers into visibility.
Dickens is using a single recurring image as a kind of structural spine — every time we see that fire, we know what it means.
It's form and feeling working together — the image carries the argument that facts alone cannot account for what Louisa is.
The fire image is genuinely one of the great sustained motifs in Victorian fiction, and it works because Dickens never over-explains it.
He trusts the reader to feel what Louisa cannot say.
And that connects to the larger question of the novel's narrative voice, which is doing something very unusual.
The narrator is simultaneously inside the satire — mocking Gradgrind, performing the mechanistic logic — and outside it, carrying the emotional counter-argument.
When Dickens describes the schoolroom at the start, he narrates it in the language of Gradgrind's system — 'a plain, bare, monotonous vault' — and that flatness is itself an indictment.
'a plain, bare, monotonous vault of a schoolroom'
The narrator has borrowed the enemy's vocabulary in order to condemn him with it — it's a formal sleight of hand that takes some nerve to pull off.
There's a term for that technique — free indirect discourse shading into satiric mimicry — but I think the more interesting question is why Dickens needs it.
He can't simply stand outside Gradgrind's world and describe it as monstrous, because the reader needs to understand the internal logic of the system — why intelligent people believed in it.
Utilitarianism wasn't villainous in intent — it was a reforming ideology, promoted by serious thinkers who genuinely wanted to improve the lives of the poor.
So Dickens has to inhabit the system's voice in order to show, from within, where it goes wrong — and that requires a narrative form that can hold both registers simultaneously.
The form is doing genuine philosophical work — it's not decoration, it's argument.
And it produces those moments of terrible, quiet irony that stay with you long after you've closed the book.
When Louisa finally breaks — when she goes back to her father and tries to articulate what he has done to her — the language becomes almost unbearably plain.
She says something to the effect that he has educated her away from every feeling that could have saved her.
'I have been endowed with so much, father, and have given you so much, only to find at last that I have spent all my unused feeling on — nothing.'
That word 'unused' — it's devastating, because it's still his language, still the language of utility and resource, turned back on him as an accusation.
The form mirrors the content right down to the word choice of a character at the moment of her collapse.
That image of a world that has made its own language inescapable — even in the act of accusation — feels like a perfect note on which to move forward.
Because that language doesn't exist in isolation — it's embedded in a place, and the place is Coketown.
That's where we're going next — how Dickens makes a town into something that feels less like a setting and more like a force pressing down on every life within it.
We've been talking about how Dickens bends the form of the novel itself to mirror the grinding machinery of Gradgrind's world.
But there's another force in this novel that shapes every character, every relationship, every breath — and that's the town itself.
Coketown isn't backdrop — it's antagonist.
What strikes me every time I return to this novel is how early Dickens commits to Coketown as a full presence.
It appears in Book One, Chapter Five, and the description isn't scenic — it's prosecutorial.
He gives us this extraordinary catalogue of sameness — the buildings all red brick, the streets all very like one another.
"It was a town of red brick, or of brick that would have been red if the smoke and ashes had allowed it."
That conditional — 'would have been red if the smoke had allowed it' — tells you everything about what this place does to natural things.
It suppresses the essential quality of a thing while leaving the husk intact.
And what Dickens captures there is historically precise, which I think we sometimes underestimate.
Preston — which was almost certainly the model for Coketown — was genuinely suffocating in the early 1850s.
The air pollution, the monotony of the factory rows, the rivers running with chemical dye — that wasn't literary hyperbole.
When Dickens describes the river as 'a black canal,' that was reportage as much as metaphor.
What interests me is the psychological mechanism — the way the town's uniformity is designed to produce uniform people.
Gradgrind's school and Bounderby's mill are not separate institutions — they're the same project, and Coketown is their physical embodiment.
What gets me — what always gets me — is the serpent imagery.
Dickens describes the pistons of the steam engines as the heads of melancholy mad elephants, which is extraordinary enough.
But then there are the smoke serpents — interminable coils of smoke issuing from tall chimneys.
"The smoke-serpents were indigenous to the place."
Indigenous — as if the pollution belongs there, as if it's the town's native creature.
It inverts the pastoral completely — instead of the land producing life, it produces choking.
And there's something almost Edenic about the word 'indigenous' — it casts the serpent as the thing that was always there, always waiting.
Caroline, that's exactly right, and it connects to something Dickens does architecturally across the whole novel.
He keeps returning to Coketown with the same phrases — it becomes a kind of leitmotif.
The repetition isn't laziness — it's formal mimicry of the town's own repetitive logic.
Every street is so like another — the description comes back the same way the factory workers return to the same looms.
The prose performs the entrapment it describes.
There's a harder point lurking here, which is about who Coketown is actually designed to trap.
Stephen Blackpool cannot leave — not economically, not legally, thanks to the divorce laws Dickens is so pointed about.
Gradgrind can leave, and does — his children can aspire to elsewhere.
The atmosphere of Coketown is not evenly distributed.
The smoke that is decorative description for a middle-class reader is a literal working condition for Stephen.
When Stephen says, in that terrible quiet way he has, that it's 'aw a muddle' — the muddle is Coketown, right down to its foundations.
"It's aw a muddle."
That phrase lands like a diagnosis — it's what the town does, and it's what the town is.
Stephen breaks my heart, honestly, more than any other character in the novel.
Because the town has shaped him into someone who can perceive injustice absolutely clearly but has no vocabulary to dismantle it.
He can't join the union — he won't — and he can't appeal to Bounderby, who only hears complaint as ingratitude.
Coketown doesn't just pollute the air — it forecloses the possibility of argument.
And Rachael — she's defined entirely by her endurance of Coketown, her grace inside the grey.
She isn't given the luxury of escape, even imaginatively — the circus world that redeems Sissy is simply not available to her.
Which is why the circus is such a bold structural move — it exists almost entirely outside Coketown's logic.
Sleary's people aren't grimy — they're colourful, they perform, they're useless in the Utilitarian sense.
And Sleary's great speech about fancy — that people must be amused — it reads as a direct rebuke to the atmosphere of the town.
"People mutht be amuthed, Thquire, thomehow."
The lisp that Dickens gives him is often read as comic, but it's also protective — it makes the sentiment harder to dismiss as sentimental.
You can't sneer at Sleary without sneering at something slightly ridiculous — and in doing so you reveal yourself.
I'll push back very gently on the circus as pure utopia, though.
Sleary's Horse-riding is also a capitalist enterprise — it travels, it charges admission, it exploits performers.
Dickens doesn't quite see that, or doesn't want to — the fancy world is romanticised in a way the factory world is not.
But that's part of what makes Coketown so powerful as a device — it's the negative space against which every other possibility is measured.
Without Coketown's grey, the circus colours mean nothing.
That tension — between the town's grey totality and the fragile, improbable colour that persists inside it — is exactly where the novel ends up.
And it brings us to the question we've been circling all episode: does Hard Times ultimately believe in softening?
Can a world this hard yield — and to what?

segments.title: Closing: Hard Times and the Possibility of Softening

utterances.text: We've spent some time with Coketown's smoke and stone — that atmosphere of relentless, grinding fact.
But the novel doesn't leave us entirely in that grey fog — and I want to end by asking what Dickens offers against it.
Is there a possibility of softening in Hard Times — and if so, where does it come from?
I think the answer to that question is Sissy Jupe — almost entirely Sissy Jupe.
She arrives in the novel as a kind of embarrassment to the Gradgrind system — she can't define a horse, she cries at school, she brings fancy into a world that has outlawed it.
And yet by the end she is the moral centre of the book.
There's a moment where Gradgrind comes to her, broken, needing help to save Louisa — and she simply helps him.
She doesn't lecture him. She doesn't extract a confession from him.
That quiet, unreasoned generosity is exactly what his philosophy cannot account for — and it's what saves what can be saved.
And Dickens is careful about what can and cannot be saved — which is one of the things that makes this novel braver than it first appears.
Louisa is not given a redemptive love story.
She doesn't end up with Harthouse reformed or with some new husband who sees her truly.
The famous closing passage gives her a life of doing good on limited ground — Dickens's phrase is extraordinary.
"Trying hard to know her humbler fellow-creatures, and to beautify their lives of machinery and reality with those imaginative graces and delights, without which the heart of infancy will wither up."
That's not a happy ending — it's a careful, honourable consolation.
And the word 'wither' carries real weight — it's the novel's diagnosis applied now as a warning forward.
What strikes me historically is that Dickens is refusing two kinds of false hope simultaneously.
He's refusing the individualist fantasy — that a good heart alone will fix a broken system.
But he's also refusing the revolutionary resolution — the workers don't rise up and overturn Bounderby's mill.
Stephen Blackpool is arguably the most politically honest figure in the book — precisely because he is destroyed without redemption.
He falls into the old Hell Shaft and he dies, and the system that killed him carries on.
His last words reach toward a star he can see from the bottom of the pit — it's one of the most devastating images in Victorian fiction.
Dickens gives him beauty and denies him justice — which is more honest than most novelists would dare to be.
That image of the star — it undoes me every time.
Stephen asks Rachael to look at it with him as he's being lifted out — he says it seemed to shine on him as a hand were stretched out.
"Often as I coom to myseln, and found it shinin' on me down there in my trouble, I thowt it were the star as guided to Our Saviour's home."
The dialect, the faith, the simplicity — Dickens is not being condescending.
He is giving Stephen the most genuine spiritual moment in the entire novel.
And it breaks your heart because it changes nothing in the world of the book.
I want to come back to Gradgrind himself, because I think his collapse is the structural pivot of the whole novel.
He built a philosophy of facts, he applied it to his own children as experiments, and it destroyed them.
Tom becomes a thief. Louisa's marriage to Bounderby is a transaction that nearly breaks her.
And when Louisa comes home to him — that scene in Book Two where she arrives in the storm — she tells him what his system has done to her.
She says she has grown up without the right to cultivate her imagination, to be young, to have any inner life at all.
"What have you done, O father, what have you done with the garden that should have bloomed once, in this great wilderness here?"
That garden against wilderness — the whole novel's argument compressed into a single image of reproach.
And Gradgrind's response to that moment is one of the few places where Dickens allows the system to feel its own failure.
He doesn't defend himself. He sits there as the walls of his philosophy come down.
By the end of the novel Dickens tells us he became known for making his facts and figures subservient to Faith, Hope, and Charity.
Now some readers find that too easy — a conversion too swift.
But I think Dickens is less interested in whether Gradgrind has genuinely changed than in establishing what the price of his philosophy was.
He paid it in his children. That's the ledger he cannot balance.
Bounderby's end is so different though — and so satisfying in a rather vindictive way.
Mrs. Sparsit has been scheming all novel to destroy Louisa in Bounderby's eyes — and instead she destroys him.
She tracks down Mrs. Pegler — this little old woman Bounderby has been suspiciously protective of — and brings her forward.
And it turns out Mrs. Pegler is his mother — the doting, devoted mother he claimed had abandoned him.
His whole self-made-man myth — the gutter, the starvation, the ditch — all of it invented.
Dickens doesn't just expose him — he lets him bluster and threaten almost to the last, which is funnier and more accurate.
Men like Bounderby never believe the exposure is final.
And then he dies, five years later, in a fit in a Coketown street — and Dickens dispatches him in a single sentence.
No deathbed, no reckoning, no final speech.
Just — gone.
That's Dickens at his most controlled — the formal economy of the ending perfectly matching the moral verdict.
He won't waste beautiful prose on a man who never deserved imagination.
What I keep returning to, thinking about this novel now, is how contemporary its central question still is.
What is education for — the cultivation of the whole human being, or the production of useful economic units?
Dickens put that question in 1854 with an urgency that hasn't dimmed.
Every generation re-encounters a version of Gradgrind standing at the front of a classroom insisting on facts.
And somewhere in that classroom, one hopes, there is still a Sissy Jupe who cannot quite be reduced.
That feels like exactly the right note on which to close.
We've moved today through Coketown's smoke and fog, through the machinery of Gradgrind's schoolroom, and arrived here — at the question of what survives all that grinding.
The answer Dickens offers is fragile, partial, and all the more honest for it.
My warmest thanks to Dr. Eleanor Hartley, whose eye for craft has illuminated every page we've touched.
To Professor James Blackstone, who has given us the history behind the fiction and the anger the fiction deserves.
And to Caroline Woodcourt, who has read this novel with her whole heart and made us feel it.
And to you, listening — thank you for spending this time with a novel that still has so much to say.
Hard Times. Unpacked.

‘Why, my dear Louisa,’ said Mr. Gradgrind,
completely recovered by this time, ‘I would advise you
(since you ask me) to consider this question, as you have been
accustomed to consider every other question, simply as one of
tangible Fact.  The ignorant and the giddy may embarrass
such subjects with irrelevant fancies, and other absurdities that
have no existence, properly viewed—really no
existence—but it is no compliment to you to say, that you
know better.  Now, what are the Facts of this case? 
You are, we will say in round numbers, twenty years of age; Mr.
Bounderby is, we will say in round numbers, fifty.  There is
some disparity in your respective years, but in your means and
positions there is none; on the contrary, there is a great
suitability.  Then the question arises, Is this one
disparity sufficient to operate as a bar to such a
marriage?  In considering this question, it is not
unimportant to take into account the statistics of marriage, so
far as they have yet been obtained, in England and Wales.  I
find, on reference to the figures, that a large proportion of
these marriages are contracted between parties of very unequal
ages, and that the elder of these contracting parties is, in
rather more than three-fourths of these instances, the
bridegroom.  It is remarkable as showing the wide prevalence
of this law, that among the natives of the British possessions in
India, also in a considerable part of China, and among the
Calmucks of Tartary, the best means of computation yet furnished
us by travellers, yield similar results.  The disparity I
have mentioned, therefore, almost ceases to be disparity, and
(virtually) all but disappears.’
c13:p21.summary: Gradgrind argues that love should be replaced with 'Fact,' then uses marriage statistics from England, Wales, India, China, and Tartary to prove the age disparity between Louisa and Bounderby is negligible and normal.

He thought that he, and some one on whom his heart had long
been set—but she was not Rachael, and that surprised him,
even in the midst of his imaginary happiness—stood in the
church being married.  While the ceremony was performing,
and while he recognized among the witnesses some whom he knew to
be living, and many whom he knew to be dead, darkness came on,
succeeded by the shining of a tremendous light.  It broke
from one line in the table of commandments at the altar, and
illuminated the building with the words.  They were sounded
through the church, too, as if there were voices in the fiery
letters.  Upon this, the whole appearance before him and
around him changed, and nothing was left as it had been, but
himself and the clergyman.  They stood in the daylight
before a crowd so vast, that if all the people in the world could
have been brought together into one space, they could not have
looked, he thought, more numerous; and they all abhorred him, and
there was not one pitying or friendly eye among the millions that
were fastened on his face.  He stood on a raised stage,
under his own loom; and, looking up at the shape the loom took,
and hearing the burial service distinctly read, he knew that he
was there to suffer death.  In an instant what he stood on
fell below him, and he was gone.

The streets were hot and dusty on the summer day, and the sun
was so bright that it even shone through the heavy vapour
drooping over Coketown, and could not be looked at
steadily.  Stokers emerged from low underground doorways
into factory yards, and sat on steps, and posts, and palings,
wiping their swarthy visages, and contemplating coals.  The
whole town seemed to be frying in oil.  There was a stifling
smell of hot oil everywhere.  The steam-engines shone with
it, the dresses of the Hands were soiled with it, the mills
throughout their many stories oozed and trickled it.  The
atmosphere of those Fairy palaces was like the breath of the
simoom: and their inhabitants, wasting with heat, toiled
languidly in the desert.  But no temperature made the
melancholy mad elephants more mad or more sane.  Their
wearisome heads went up and down at the same rate, in hot weather
and cold, wet weather and dry, fair weather and foul.  The
measured motion of their shadows on the walls, was the substitute
Coketown had to show for the shadows of rustling woods; while,
for the summer hum of insects, it could offer, all the year
round, from the dawn of Monday to the night of Saturday, the
whirr of shafts and wheels.

The scene was a plain, bare, monotonous vault of a
school-room, and the speaker’s square forefinger emphasized
his observations by underscoring every sentence with a line on
the schoolmaster’s sleeve.  The emphasis was helped by
the speaker’s square wall of a forehead, which had his
eyebrows for its base, while his eyes found commodious cellarage
in two dark caves, overshadowed by the wall.  The emphasis
was helped by the speaker’s mouth, which was wide, thin,
and hard set.  The emphasis was helped by the
speaker’s voice, which was inflexible, dry, and
dictatorial.  The emphasis was helped by the speaker’s
hair, which bristled on the skirts of his bald head, a plantation
of firs to keep the wind from its shining surface, all covered
with knobs, like the crust of a plum pie, as if the head had
scarcely warehouse-room for the hard facts stored inside. 
The speaker’s obstinate carriage, square coat, square legs,
square shoulders,—nay, his very neckcloth, trained to take
him by the throat with an unaccommodating grasp, like a stubborn
fact, as it was,—all helped the emphasis.

c14:p32.text:
‘Ladies and gentlemen, I am Josiah Bounderby of
Coketown.  Since you have done my wife and myself the honour
of drinking our healths and happiness, I suppose I must
acknowledge the same; though, as you all know me, and know what I
am, and what my extraction was, you won’t expect a speech
from a man who, when he sees a Post, says “that’s a
Post,” and when he sees a Pump, says “that’s a
Pump,” and is not to be got to call a Post a Pump, or a
Pump a Post, or either of them a Toothpick.  If you want a
speech this morning, my friend and father-in-law, Tom Gradgrind,
is a Member of Parliament, and you know where to get it.  I
am not your man.  However, if I feel a little independent
when I look around this table to-day, and reflect how little I
thought of marrying Tom Gradgrind’s daughter when I was a
ragged street-boy, who never washed his face unless it was at a
pump, and that not oftener than once a fortnight, I hope I may be
excused.  So, I hope you like my feeling independent; if you
don’t, I can’t help it.  I  do  feel
independent.  Now I have mentioned, and you have mentioned,
that I am this day married to Tom Gradgrind’s
daughter.  I am very glad to be so.  It has long been
my wish to be so.  I have watched her bringing-up, and I
believe she is worthy of me.  At the same time—not to
deceive you—I believe I am worthy of her.  So, I thank
you, on both our parts, for the good-will you have shown towards
us; and the best wish I can give the unmarried part of the
present company, is this: I hope every bachelor may find as good
a wife as I have found.  And I hope every spinster may find
as good a husband as my wife has found.’

Seen from a distance in such weather, Coketown lay shrouded in
a haze of its own, which appeared impervious to the sun’s
rays.  You only knew the town was there, because you knew
there could have been no such sulky blotch upon the prospect
without a town.  A blur of soot and smoke, now confusedly
tending this way, now that way, now aspiring to the vault of
Heaven, now murkily creeping along the earth, as the wind rose
and fell, or changed its quarter: a dense formless jumble, with
sheets of cross light in it, that showed nothing but masses of
darkness:—Coketown in the distance was suggestive of
itself, though not a brick of it could be seen.

with her in her small neat room.  All day, Rachael toiled as
such people must toil, whatever their anxieties.  The
smoke-serpents were indifferent who was lost or found, who turned
out bad or good; the melancholy mad elephants, like the Hard Fact
men, abated nothing of their set routine, whatever
happened.  Day and night again, day and night again. 
The monotony was unbroken.  Even Stephen Blackpool’s
disappearance was falling into the general way, and becoming as
monotonous a wonder as any piece of machinery in Coketown.

But, happy Sissy’s happy children loving her; all
children loving her; she, grown learned in childish lore;
thinking no innocent and pretty fancy ever to be despised; trying
hard to know her humbler fellow-creatures, and to beautify their
lives of machinery and reality with those imaginative graces and
delights, without which the heart of infancy will wither up, the
sturdiest physical manhood will be morally stark death, and the
plainest national prosperity figures can show, will be the
Writing on the Wall,—she holding this course as part of no
fantastic vow, or bond, or brotherhood, or sisterhood, or pledge,
or covenant, or fancy dress, or fancy fair; but simply as a duty

He held the respectable office of general spy and informer in
the establishment, for which volunteer service he received a
present at Christmas, over and above his weekly wage.  He
had grown into an extremely clear-headed, cautious, prudent young
man, who was safe to rise in the world.  His mind was so
exactly regulated, that he had no affections or passions. 
All his proceedings were the result of the nicest and coldest
calculation; and it was not without cause that Mrs. Sparsit
habitually observed of him, that he was a young man of the
steadiest principle she had ever known.  Having satisfied
himself, on his father’s death, that his mother had a right
of settlement in Coketown, this excellent young economist had
asserted that right for her with such a steadfast adherence to
the principle of the case, that she had been shut up in the
workhouse ever since.  It must be admitted that he allowed
her half a pound of tea a year, which was weak in him: first,
because all gifts have an inevitable tendency to pauperise the
recipient, and secondly, because his only reasonable transaction
in that commodity would have been to buy it for as little as he
could possibly give, and sell it for as much as he could possibly
get; it having been clearly ascertained by philosophers that in
this is comprised the whole duty of man—not a part of
man’s duty, but the whole.

c2:p47.text:
So, Mr. M’Choakumchild began in his best manner. 
He and some one hundred and forty other schoolmasters, had been
lately turned at the same time, in the same factory, on the same
principles, like so many pianoforte legs.  He had been put
through an immense variety of paces, and had answered volumes of
head-breaking questions.  Orthography, etymology, syntax,
and prosody, biography, astronomy, geography, and general
cosmography, the sciences of compound proportion, algebra,
land-surveying and levelling, vocal music, and drawing from
models, were all at the ends of his ten chilled fingers.  He
had worked his stony way into Her Majesty’s most Honourable
Privy Council’s Schedule B, and had taken the bloom off the
higher branches of mathematics and physical science, French,
German, Latin, and Greek.  He knew all about all the Water
Sheds of all the world (whatever they are), and all the histories
of all the peoples, and all the names of all the rivers and
mountains, and all the productions, manners, and customs of all
the countries, and all their boundaries and bearings on the two
and thirty points of the compass.  Ah, rather overdone,
M’Choakumchild.  If he had only learnt a little less,
how infinitely better he might have taught much more!

Morgiana in the Forty Thieves: looking into all the vessels
ranged before him, one after another, to see what they
contained.  Say, good M’Choakumchild.  When from

No word of a new marriage had ever passed between them; but
Rachael had taken great pity on him years ago, and to her alone
he had opened his closed heart all this time, on the subject of
his  p.
63 miseries; and he knew very well that if he were free to
ask her, she would take him.  He thought of the home he
might at that moment have been seeking with pleasure and pride;
of the different man he might have been that night; of the
lightness then in his now heavy-laden breast; of the then
restored honour, self-respect, and tranquillity all torn to
pieces.  He thought of the waste of the best part of his
life, of the change it made in his character for the worse every
day, of the dreadful nature of his existence, bound hand and
foot, to a dead woman, and tormented by a demon in her
shape.  He thought of Rachael, how young when they were
first brought together in these circumstances, how mature now,
how soon to grow old.  He thought of the number of girls and
women she had seen marry, how many homes with children in them
she had seen grow up around her, how she had contentedly pursued
her own lone quiet path—for him—and how he had
sometimes seen a shade of melancholy on her blessed face, that
smote him with remorse and despair.  He set the picture of
her up, beside the infamous image of last night; and thought,
Could it be, that the whole earthly course of one so gentle,
good, and self-denying, was subjugate to such a wretch as

c23:p72.text:
Slackbridge, the delegate, had to address his audience too
that night; and Slackbridge had obtained a clean bill from the
printer, and had brought it in his pocket.  Oh, my friends
and fellow-countrymen, the down-trodden operatives of Coketown,
oh, my fellow-brothers and fellow-workmen and fellow-citizens and
fellow-men, what a to-do was there, when Slackbridge unfolded
what he called ‘that damning document,’ and held it
up to the gaze, and for the execration of the working-man
community!  ‘Oh, my fellow-men, behold of what a
traitor in the camp of those great spirits who are enrolled upon
the holy scroll of Justice and of Union, is appropriately
capable!  Oh, my prostrate friends, with the galling yoke of
tyrants on your necks and the iron foot of despotism treading
down your fallen forms into the dust of the earth, upon which
right glad would your oppressors be to see you creeping on your
bellies all the days of your lives, like the serpent in the
garden—oh, my brothers, and shall I as a man not add, my
sisters too, what do you say,  now , of Stephen Blackpool,
with a slight stoop in his shoulders and about five foot seven in
height, as set forth in this degrading and disgusting document,
this blighting bill, this pernicious placard, this abominable
advertisement; and with what majesty of denouncement will you
crush the viper, who would bring this stain and shame upon the
God-like race that happily has cast him out for ever!  Yes,
my compatriots, happily cast him out and sent him forth! 
For you remember how he stood here before you on this platform;
you remember how, face to face and foot to foot, I pursued him
through all his intricate windings; you remember how he sneaked
and slunk, and sidled, and splitted of straws, until, with not an
inch of ground to which to cling, I hurled him out from amongst
us: an object for the undying finger of scorn to point at, and
for the avenging fire of every free and thinking mind to scorch
and scar!  And now, my friends—my labouring friends,
for I rejoice and triumph in that stigma—my friends whose
hard but honest beds are made in toil, and whose scanty but
independent pots are boiled in hardship; and now, I say, my
friends, what appellation has that dastard craven taken to
himself, when, with the mask torn from his features, he stands
before us in all his native deformity, a What?  A
thief!  A plunderer!  A proscribed fugitive, with a
price upon his head; a fester and a wound upon the noble
character of the Coketown operative!  Therefore, my band of
brothers in a sacred bond, to which your children and your
children’s children yet unborn have set their infant hands
and seals, I propose to you on the part of the United Aggregate
Tribunal, ever watchful for your welfare, ever zealous for your
benefit, that this meeting does Resolve: That Stephen Blackpool,
weaver, referred to in this placard, having been already solemnly
disowned by the community of Coketown Hands, the same are free
from the shame of his misdeeds, and cannot as a class be
reproached with his dishonest actions!’

c25:p68.text:
They carried him very gently along the fields, and down the
lanes, and over the wide landscape; Rachael always holding the
hand in hers.  Very few whispers broke the mournful
silence.  It was soon a funeral procession.  The star
had shown him where to find the God of the poor; and through
humility, and sorrow, and forgiveness, he had gone to his
Redeemer’s rest.
